questions.q: A restaurant asks you for "a function that splits the bill between friends". What should you do before writing any code?
questions.explain: The method starts on paper: understand, inputs, outputs, edge cases, pseudocode. Questions like "what if there are 0 friends?" or "who pays the leftover kobo?" are cheap to answer now and expensive to discover later.
options: Write the function quickly, then see which inputs break it
Name the inputs, the output and the edge cases, such as 0 friends or a bill that does not divide evenly
Look up a bill-splitting library
Write the tests by copying what a first version prints

questions.q: You are writing averageScore(scores) for a class. Which input is an edge case that needs its own decision?
questions.explain: An empty class means dividing by zero students. The function must decide what to return (for example "no average"), and a test should record that decision. The other options are normal cases.
options: A class with 30 students
A class where every score is between 40 and 90
A class with no students at all
A class where the scores are whole numbers

questions.q: Why does if (n % 2 === 1) return "odd"; return "even"; call -3 even?
questions.explain: In JavaScript the remainder keeps the sign of the left number: -3 % 2 is -1. Comparing with 0 (n % 2 === 0 means even) works for every sign.
options: Because % does not work on negative numbers
Because -3 % 2 is -1, so the comparison with 1 is false
Because -3 is not a whole number
Because === ignores the minus sign

questions.q: A largest-of-three function starts with let best = 0; and then replaces best with any bigger input. Which test exposes the bug?
questions.explain: With all negative inputs nothing is bigger than 0, so it returns 0, which is not one of the inputs. Start with the first input instead: it is a real candidate.
options: largest(3, 9, 4)
largest(9, 9, 9)
largest(-4, -1, -9)
largest(0, 5, 2)

questions.q: A grade function checks score >= 40 (E) first, then score >= 45 (D), and so on up to score >= 70 (A), returning at the first match. What grade does a score of 95 get?
questions.explain: 95 is at least 40, so the very first check matches and returns E. With a chain of >= checks, go from the highest grade down, so each check only sees scores that failed the ones above.
options: A
E
F
invalid

questions.q: Delivery is free when the goods cost ₦20,000 or more. Prices are in kobo. Which pair of tests best checks this rule?
questions.explain: A boundary pair tests one value exactly on the limit and one just past it. It is the only way to tell >= from >: both give the same answer for ₦5,000 and ₦50,000.
options: A ₦5,000 cart and a ₦50,000 cart
A cart of exactly 2,000,000 kobo and one of 1,999,999 kobo
An empty cart and a ₦20,000 cart
Two different ₦30,000 carts

questions.q: An ATM function checks "amount is more than the balance" before "amount is a positive whole number". What goes wrong?
questions.explain: All checks must still pass, so the same requests are refused. But the first failing check decides the message. Check whether the request makes sense at all before you look at the account.
options: Valid withdrawals are refused
Negative withdrawals are approved
Some bad requests get a misleading message, such as "insufficient funds" for ₦5,000,000.5
Nothing: the order of the checks never matters

questions.q: Why does ageOn take today's date as parameters instead of reading the computer's clock?
questions.explain: A function that reads the clock gives a different answer every day. Making time an input keeps the function predictable and testable; the real program passes in the clock's date at its very edge.
options: JavaScript cannot read the current date
So the same inputs always give the same answer, and a test written today still passes next year
Because reading the clock is slow
So the user can lie about their age

questions.q: Why does the workshop store ₦149.99 as 14999?
questions.explain: Decimal fractions are stored approximately, so sums drift by tiny amounts. Whole kobo are exact. You divide by 100 only to display the amount.
options: Whole numbers use less memory
Adding and subtracting whole kobo is always exact, while decimals like 149.99 are not stored exactly
Because toFixed only works on whole numbers
Banks require it by law

questions.q: A test fails with FAIL body heat: got 97.88000000000001, expected 97.88. What is the best fix?
questions.explain: The formula is right; decimals are stored approximately. Decide what precision matters and compare at that precision. Copying the strange number into the test would lock in an accident, not a requirement.
options: Change the formula until the result is exactly 97.88
Delete the test: decimals cannot be tested
Round both values to the precision a person cares about (one or two decimals) before comparing
Change the expected value to 97.88000000000001

questions.q: With the workshop's made-up bands (first ₦800,000 at 0%, next ₦2,200,000 at 15%, the rest at 20%), how much tax does someone earning ₦3,500,000 pay?
questions.explain: ₦0 on the first ₦800,000, 15% of ₦2,200,000 = ₦330,000, and 20% of the last ₦500,000 = ₦100,000. Total ₦430,000. Only the slice above each line pays the higher rate; 20% of the whole income (₦700,000) is the classic misunderstanding.

questions.q: A cart function adds ₦1,500 delivery whenever the subtotal is below ₦20,000. What does it charge for an empty cart, and is that right?
questions.explain: 0 is below ₦20,000, so the rule charges delivery for nothing. The empty cart needs its own rule, which is why "empty input" belongs in every edge-case table.
options: ₦0, which is right
₦1,500, which is wrong: nothing is being delivered
It crashes, because an empty list has no items
₦20,000, the free-delivery threshold

questions.q: The grading scale says "B: 60–69, A: 70–100" and nothing about 69.5. What should you do?
questions.explain: When the problem statement leaves a gap, you have to make a decision. Writing it down and recording it in a test means the next developer knows it was on purpose, and can check it with whoever owns the rules.
options: Assume scores are always whole numbers and move on
Let the program crash on 69.5 so someone notices
Decide a rule (for example "the grade whose lower limit it has reached"), write it down and add a test for 69.5
Round every score up before grading

questions.q: Where should the expected value in a test come from?
questions.explain: A test compares the program with your understanding of the problem. Copying the program's own output only proves the program agrees with itself, bugs included.
options: From running the function once and copying what it prints
From working the answer out by hand, from the problem's rules
From the largest value the function can return
It does not matter, as long as the test passes

questions.q: The password checker returns a list of problems instead of true or false. Why?
questions.explain: The output was chosen from the requirement. A boolean says "no" without saying why; a list of problems gives every reason, and its length tells you whether there are any.
options: Lists are faster to check than booleans
The form must tell the user everything that is wrong at once, and an empty list still means "acceptable"
JavaScript functions cannot return booleans
So the password can be stored in the list

questions.q: What is a guard clause?
questions.explain: if (!Number.isInteger(amount) || amount <= 0) return "Declined: invalid amount"; is a guard clause. Bad cases leave first; only valid input reaches the main logic.
options: A comment that explains a function's rules
A test that must pass before code is shipped
A check at the top of a function that returns early for bad input, so the rest can trust its input
A loop that stops at the first problem

questions.q: Why does the parity problem include a test with "4" (in quotes)?
questions.explain: Text that looks like a number is one of the most common inputs a real program meets. Number.isInteger("4") is false, so the function answers "invalid" instead of guessing.
options: To check that the function can read text aloud
Because values from forms and web addresses arrive as text, and "4" is not a number
Because "4" is an odd number in JavaScript
To make the test list longer

questions.q: The leap-year rule is: divisible by 4, except years divisible by 100, unless also divisible by 400. Which set of test years covers every part of the rule?
questions.explain: 2024 (by 4: leap), 2026 (not by 4), 1900 (by 100 but not 400: not leap) and 2000 (by 400: leap). Each part of the rule gets at least one test; the other sets leave parts untested.

questions.q: Someone writes f - 32 * 5 / 9 for Fahrenheit to Celsius. What happens?
questions.explain: As in school maths, * and / run before -. The formula needs (f - 32) * 5 / 9. A known test like 212 °F = 100 °C catches the mistake at once.
options: The same result, because JavaScript reads left to right
It multiplies and divides first, so it subtracts about 17.8 instead of subtracting 32 first
A syntax error
It only works for negative temperatures

questions.q: A promotion gives "20% off, up to ₦5,000 off". Which price shows that the cap is working?
questions.explain: 20% of ₦40,000 is ₦8,000, over the cap, so the discount must become ₦5,000. At ₦10,000 or ₦20,000 the discount is under the cap and the cap never runs.

questions.q: Why does the cart refuse an item with quantity -2 instead of just adding it?
questions.explain: −2 × price is a negative amount, so the total goes down. Invalid input that changes money is a security problem, not just a bug: refuse it.
options: Negative numbers cannot be multiplied
It would reduce the bill, which lets a customer pay less than the goods cost
Because -2 is not a whole number
Because the loop cannot handle it

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The remainder keeps the sign of the left number, so -7 % 2 is -1. Zero divides by 2 with nothing left over. This is why "even" should be tested as n % 2 === 0.

questions.q: The checks are in the wrong order. What does this print?
questions.explain: Any score of 40 or more matches the first check, so 85 and 55 both get E. The later checks are never reached for them. Order the checks from the highest grade down.
options: E E F
A C F
E C F
A E F

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: For all-negative inputs nothing beats the starting value 0, so the function returns 0, which is not one of the inputs. Starting with best = a fixes it.

questions.q: This ATM checks the balance first. What does it print?
questions.explain: −500 is not more than 1000, so it passes the first check and is caught by the second. Exactly the balance is not "more than" it, so it is approved and leaves ₦0.
options:
Declined: insufficient funds
Declined: invalid amount
Approved: ₦0 left

Declined: insufficient funds
Approved: ₦1500 left
Approved: ₦0 left

Declined: insufficient funds
Declined: invalid amount
Declined: insufficient funds

Declined: invalid amount
Declined: invalid amount
Approved: ₦0 left

questions.q: This age function only subtracts the years. What does it print for someone born on 25 December 2008, on 24 September 2026 and on 25 December 2026?
questions.explain: In September the birthday has not happened yet, so the person is still 17; the naive version says 18. On the birthday itself the day is not earlier, so the correct function gives 18.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: "abc" breaks both rules. "abcdefgh" is exactly 8 characters (long enough) but has no digit. "abcdefg1" passes. The empty string has length 0 and no characters for the loop, so both problems are reported.
options: short+no digit no digit OK short+no digit
short no digit OK short
short+no digit no digit OK OK
short+no digit OK OK short+no digit

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: An empty cart has subtotal 0, which is below the threshold, so this version charges delivery for nothing: the bug the workshop's extra rule fixes. The second cart is exactly 2,000,000 kobo and >= makes delivery free.

questions.q: Amounts are in naira here. What does this print?
Prices are in kobo. What does this print?
questions.explain: 15% of 999 is 149.85 kobo, which rounds to 150, leaving 849. 0% changes nothing. 110% is refused by the guard clause before any maths runs.
options: 849 1000 invalid
849.15 1000 invalid

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 0.1 + 0.2 is not exactly 0.3 in a computer, so === fails. Rounding to one decimal first gives exactly 0.3, and the test passes.
options:
FAIL sum: got 0.30000000000000004, expected 0.3
PASS rounded sum

PASS sum
PASS rounded sum

FAIL sum: got 0.30000000000000004, expected 0.3
FAIL rounded sum: got 0.30000000000000004, expected 0.3

PASS sum
FAIL rounded sum: got 0.3, expected 0.3

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: These are the known values worth testing: boiling (100 °C = 212 °F), the point where both scales agree (−40), and freezing (32 °F = 0 °C). (c) => … is a short way to write a function, which the JavaScript course covers.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Math.floor(3500 / 1000) is 3 and the remainder 500 is one ₦500 note. ₦500 needs no ₦1,000 note. ₦4,000 leaves no remainder.

questions.q: Finish parity(n): return "invalid" when n is not a whole number, otherwise "even" or "odd". It must be correct for negative numbers too.
questions.explain: Number.isInteger refuses decimals and text. Comparing the remainder with 0 works for every sign, because -3 % 2 is -1, not 1.

questions.q: Write smallest(a, b, c) with the "keep the best so far" pattern: start with the first input, then replace it with anything smaller.
questions.explain: Starting with a (not with 0 or some big number) means the answer is always one of the inputs. The tests put the smallest value in each position, include negatives and a three-way tie.

questions.q: A cinema charges ₦1,500 for children under 12, ₦2,000 for people aged 60 or more, and ₦3,000 for everyone else. Ages must be whole numbers from 0 up; anything else is "invalid". Write ticketPrice(age) returning the price in naira.
questions.explain: The tests are boundary pairs: 11/12 for the child price and 59/60 for the senior price, plus two invalid inputs. "Under 12" is < 12; "60 or more" is >= 60.

questions.q: A username must be 3 to 15 characters long and contain no spaces. Write usernameProblems(name) that returns a list of problems, and the report line prints OK when the list is empty. Use "too short", "too long" and "has a space".
questions.explain: Each rule adds its own problem, so the user sees all of them at once. "ada" is exactly 3 characters, the lower boundary, and passes. The flag pattern finds a space by looking at each character.
questions.expected:
OK
too short
has a space
too long, has a space

questions.q: A bank charges ₦10 for transfers up to and including ₦5,000, ₦25 for transfers up to and including ₦50,000, and ₦50 above that. Amounts must be positive; otherwise return "invalid". Write transferFee(amount).
questions.explain: "Up to and including" means <=. Checking from the smallest band up works here because each check uses <=: an amount only reaches a check after failing the smaller ones.

questions.q: Finish cartTotal(items): add up price × quantity for every item (prices in kobo), then add 150000 kobo delivery unless the cart is empty or the subtotal is at least 2000000 kobo.
questions.explain: The empty cart gets its own rule before the delivery rule, so it costs nothing. 2 × 250,000 = 500,000 plus delivery is 650,000; the last cart is exactly the free-delivery threshold.

questions.q: Write ageOn(birthYear, birthMonth, birthDay, year, month, day): subtract the years, then take one away if the birthday has not happened yet in year.
questions.explain: The birthday has not happened when the month is earlier, or the month is the same and the day is earlier. The tests cover the day before, the day itself, an earlier month and a later month.

questions.q: Write toCelsius(f) that converts Fahrenheit to Celsius and rounds the result to one decimal place.
questions.explain: The parentheses make the subtraction happen first. Multiplying by 10, rounding and dividing by 10 keeps one decimal: 0 °F is −17.777…, shown as −17.8.
